text:
Marathon Petroleum rose slightly today, but the stock is down sharply from its peak two weeks ago—it fell nearly $34 per share between September 17 and September 22. The main driver of this week's decline is falling oil prices: crude dropped Friday on reports of a potential diplomatic deal between the U.S. and Iran to ease the Persian Gulf standoff, which has been pushing prices higher. When crude falls, refiners typically see tighter margins between what they pay for oil and what they make selling refined products like gasoline and diesel.

The stock's weakness reflects genuine pressure on refining economics. U.S. oil is trading at $96 per barrel versus $114 for global crude—a wide gap that suggests lower demand for U.S. refined products. Meanwhile, refineries are running near full capacity at 94%, and both gasoline and diesel inventories remain substantial, limiting pricing power. Even if a diesel export ban were enacted to support prices, that benefit would be fleeting as refiners respond by cutting production.
